surface_forms: meilleure amie de la fille de ce Vinteuil

appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus's tirade on Bloch's father living at "la Commanderie" and rue des Blancs-Manteaux ("Mais un Juif !... Quel sadisme !" / "quel comble de perversité"), seconded by Morel's aside "C'est bien d'un youpin !"
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus's extended, contemptuous tirade recasts Bloch and his family as sacrilegious intruders on noble- and church-coded ground, and Morel's slur reinforces the same contempt; the narrator's own framing of the speech as ambiguously 'antijuif ou prohébreu' keeps full narratorial endorsement uncertain.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Derrière Albertine je ne voyais plus les montagnes bleues de la mer, mais la chambre de Montjouvain où elle tombait dans les bras de Mlle Vinteuil"; "La vérité de ce que Cottard m'avait dit... ne faisait plus doute pour moi... c'était vrai !"
appraisal_events.explanation: Once Albertine reveals her closeness to l'amie de Mlle Vinteuil, the narrator becomes convinced of her intimacy with that circle and recasts her, in his own endorsed judgment, through the degrading image of Mlle Vinteuil's remembered liaison at Montjouvain.

status_effects.explanation: Bloch is subjected to sustained mockery and antisemitic stereotyping from Charlus, seconded by Morel, locally lowering how he is regarded in the scene.
Charlus's tirade repeatedly casts Bloch and his family as unworthy 'profaners' of aristocratic- and church-coded spaces, symbolically excluding them from that world.
In the narrator's own judgment her standing collapses once he becomes convinced of her intimacy with Mlle Vinteuil's circle, replacing his earlier image of her with a degrading one.
As a direct consequence of the revelation, the narrator resolves to keep her from being alone and to isolate her from her own social world, curtailing her independence.
Throughout the exchange Charlus controls the conversation - feigning indifference, cutting off Brichot, and extracting Bloch's address - demonstrating unchallenged conversational dominance.

ambiguities: Charlus's tirade against Bloch is explicitly framed by the narrator as 'discours antijuif ou prohébreu — selon qu'on s'attachera à l'extérieur des phrases ou aux intentions qu'elles recelaient,' leaving open whether the passage endorses, merely reports, or itself exposes and undercuts Charlus's judgment of Bloch.
